title: Put some distance between you and your phone
description: You do not need more willpower with your phone; you need more metres — distance is the simplest focus tool there is.

body.heading: Within reach means within mind
paragraphs: A phone on the desk is not neutral, even face down and silent. Part of your attention keeps a small tab open on it: has anything arrived, should I check, what if it is important? That tab runs all day and quietly taxes everything else.

The good news is that the effect fades with distance. A phone in a bag is easier to ignore than one on the desk. A phone in another room is easier still. You are not banning anything — you are just making the check cost a short walk.

body.heading: Start with one pocket of the day
paragraphs: Choose a single stretch to practise with: the first hour of the morning, mealtimes, or your deepest work block. Charge the phone somewhere specific and slightly inconvenient during that stretch, and tell anyone who might urgently need you how else to reach you.
Expect the first days to feel odd. Your hand may pat your pocket on its own. That feeling fades quickly, and many people are surprised by how calm the borrowed hour feels.

body.heading: Make distance the default, not the exception
paragraphs: Give the phone a home that is not your pocket: a shelf by the door, a drawer in the kitchen. When it lives somewhere, picking it up becomes a small decision instead of a reflex.
None of this requires a dumbphone or a dramatic digital detox. It is the same environment trick as the biscuit tin in the cupboard — a few steps of distance, working quietly in your favour all day.

takeaway: Do not fight the phone. Just let it live a few metres further away.
